title: Camera-based AI feedback on 100 Spin e-scooters in Santa Monica cuts time ridden on sidewalks by 22% in a randomized field test
summary: Camera-based computer vision from an unnamed maker detected sidewalk riding on Spin e-scooters in Santa Monica; its feedback cut time ridden on sidewalks by 22% in a randomized test.
account: GeekWire's Todd Bishop reported on 28 July 2021 that Spin's earlier camera sidewalk detection in Seattle, built with Drover AI, consistently mistook the Burke-Gilman Trail for a sidewalk on his test rides. Spin said that it would fix the fault. Mohammad Mehdi Oshanreh, Daniel Malarkey and Don MacKenzie partnered with the operator Spin. They fitted 100 shared e-scooters in Santa Monica, California with a camera-based computer-vision system. It classifies the riding surface (sidewalk, roadway or bike lane) without the Global Positioning System (GPS). On detecting sidewalk riding, it issues in-app notifications, audible beeps and a speed reduction. From 23 November 2022, 50 of the 100 scooters were randomly selected to have the feedback disabled, with riders unaware of assignment. Data were collected until 14 February 2023. Targeted theft of camera-equipped scooters led Spin to withdraw them, limiting the sample. The authors published their results in Findings on 20 November 2024. The paper's abstract cites 488 trips and its methods section 456 trips for analysis (289 with feedback, 167 without). The feedback group spent 22% less time and 20% less distance on sidewalks and 5% more time on streets. The authors used Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and a logistic regression. They found that feedback reduced transitions from street to sidewalk. They found no such reduction in transitions from bike lane to sidewalk. About 10% of trips in both groups spent over 60% of their time on sidewalks. The paper does not name the camera system's maker. Funding came from the U.S. Department of Transportation through the C2SMART Center.
purpose: The camera system was built to detect sidewalk riding in real time and discourage it through alerts and speed limits.
system: Camera-based computer-vision riding-surface detection with in-app notifications, audible beeps and speed reduction on Spin shared e-scooters (maker not named in the paper)

Targeted theft of camera-equipped scooters led Spin to withdraw them, limiting the sample. The authors published their results in Findings on 20 November 2024. The paper's abstract cites 488 trips and its methods section 456 trips for analysis (289 with feedback, 167 without). The feedback group spent 22% less time and 20% less distance on sidewalks and 5% more time on streets. The authors used Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests and a logistic regression. They found that feedback reduced transitions from street to sidewalk. They found no such reduction in transitions from bike lane to sidewalk. About 10% of trips in both groups spent over 60% of their time on sidewalks. The paper does not name the camera system's maker. Funding came from the U.S. Department of Transportation through the C2SMART Center.
